clue.text: Blunder of large proportions by a brown fellow leads one to digress

parts.note: a goof is a silly mistake or blunder
something of large proportions is fat
tan is a light brown colour
a gent is a gentleman, a fellow

explanation.surface: A huge mistake by a suntanned man sends someone off the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' and 'leads one to' only join the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To veer suddenly off at a tangent is an idiom for wandering away from the subject, which is what digressing means.

clue.text: Have a bath when one shouldn't

definitions.text: Have a bath when one shouldn't

parts.words: Have a bath when one shouldn't
parts.note: read literally, this is climbing into heated bathwater at the wrong moment; the idiom means landing oneself in trouble

explanation.walkthrough: The literal bath is the joke: the phrase is an idiom for getting into trouble, which is what doing something you shouldn't brings.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means landing in trouble, and taking a bath of heated water when forbidden is a literal version of that.

clue.text: Old bishop at old city may show sanctity

parts.note: Odo was the eleventh-century Bishop of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A medieval bishop in an ancient city might display holiness.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'odour of sanctity' is the sweet smell said to come from a saint's body, so this scent may show that someone was holy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'the odour of sanctity' names a fragrance believed to show a person's holiness, so a scent may show sanctity.

clue.text: Crave to enter payment cut to point on shield

indicators.note: to enter means one piece goes inside another, here the craving inside the payment

parts.note: a fee is a payment for services
to itch for something is to crave it

explanation.surface: A craving to get into a payment that has been trimmed down.
explanation.walkthrough: A heraldic term: a cross whose lower limb is sharpened to a point is described this way on a coat of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry the term describes a cross or charge whose lower end is sharpened to a point, a shield-design word.

clue.text: Results of disaster from Sumatra

indicators.note: disaster signals the letters of the island's name being wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: The aftermath of a catastrophe on the Indonesian island.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the island's name, wrecked by 'disaster', gives the shocks that follow such an event, as after the 2004 tsunami off Sumatra.
explanation.definitionFit: Traumas are emotional shocks and injuries, the lasting results that follow a disaster.

clue.text: Cat with hat said to be a draw

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

indicators.note: said signals that the hat's name is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a bowler is a hard round felt hat, the British name for a derby

explanation.surface: A cat in a hat is described as an attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' joins the pieces to the definition. BOWLER (a hard round hat, the British name for a derby) spoken aloud gives BOLA.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombola is a raffle-style lottery in which tickets are pulled from a drum, so it is a kind of prize draw.

clue.text: Blue blood flowed when got at

parts.note: a nob is a toff, someone of aristocratic blue blood
bled means flowed out, as blood does

explanation.surface: Aristocratic blood was spilt when someone was attacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got at' is British slang for tampered with or bribed, as a racehorse or juror is; 'when' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To nobble a horse or a juror is to tamper with or bribe them, which is what having been got at means.

clue.text: One of us, if used, could be new or little

definitions.text: One of us, if used, could be new or little

parts.words: One of us, if used, could be new or little
parts.note: the Guardian's British readers are natives of England; with New in front the word means a New England native, with Little a narrow nationalist

explanation.walkthrough: 'One of us' is an English person to a British paper; Little Englander (an insular nationalist) and New Englander (from the north-east USA) are the qualified forms.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of England is one of the British paper's own readers, and adding New or Little gives two familiar compounds.

clue.text: Father's musician, mother's poet — spin off is pig nicker

definitions.text: Father's musician, mother's poet — spin off is pig nicker

parts.words: Father's musician, mother's poet — spin off is pig nicker
parts.note: the boy of the nursery rhyme is the offspring of a piper, comes from Mother Goose verse, and stole a pig and ran away

explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme the boy's father is a piper (a musician), the verse is a Mother Goose rhyme, and the son 'stole a pig and away he run'; 'nicker' is British slang for a thief.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery rhyme describes the son of a piper who stole a pig, so he is a pig thief with a musician father.

clue.text: Some trawl a long way from land — a mile — to find a supply of fish

indicators.note: some means only part of the following word is used, its opening letters

parts.note: out far describes a boat a long way from land
m is the abbreviation for a mile

explanation.surface: A trawler goes far offshore, a mile out, to find a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes TR, the opening of 'trawl'; 'to find' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A trout farm breeds and raises fish for sale, so it is a source of supply of fish.

clue.text: Sticky method of expostulation

definitions.meaning: read as 'by means of glue', the phrase describes a sticky way of doing something
a northern English exclamation of surprise or protest

explanation.walkthrough: Split as two words, the phrase means 'using gum', a sticky method; together it is a mild Yorkshire oath.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a dated northern English exclamation, a mild oath used to protest or express surprise.

clue.text: Rothman in trouble near Westward Ho!

indicators.note: in trouble signals that the man's surname is disturbed and rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Rothman gets into difficulty close to a Devon resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Northam is a small town in north Devon beside the seaside village of Westward Ho!, named after the Charles Kingsley novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Northam is a Devon town lying right next to the village of Westward Ho!, so it is located near that place.

clue.text: Receptacle for lubricant for what I swear is about one pound

indicators.note: is about means the vow goes around the other pieces

parts.note: an oath is what one swears
one is the Roman numeral I
lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight

explanation.surface: Asking which container holds oil, someone swears it holds about a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil bath is a container of oil in which machine parts run or are cleaned, a receptacle for lubricant.

clue.text: Countries replacing article in a wash for every Tom, Dick and Harry

indicators.note: replacing means one piece is swapped in where another stood

parts.note: laundry is the washing
a is the indefinite article
lands are countries

explanation.surface: Countries swapping an item in the wash for ordinary people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' names the letter A, which is the thing 'replacing' swaps out of the wash; the clue's own 'a' stands at the front, and 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Every Tom, Dick and Harry' is an idiom for ordinary people without distinction, as is the answer phrase meaning everyone.

clue.text: Keep down work by journalists

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
the press means journalists collectively

explanation.surface: Suppress the work of reporters.
explanation.definitionFit: To oppress people is to hold them down by force or unjust rule, which is keeping them down.

clue.text: Ancient satirist varying in posture

indicators.note: varying signals the letters are altered into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: An old writer of satire keeps changing his stance.
explanation.walkthrough: Petronius was the Roman author of the Satyricon in Nero's time.
explanation.definitionFit: Petronius wrote the Satyricon, a Roman satirical novel, so he is a satirist of the ancient world.

clue.text: See 13
Dead, possibly — sending back dessert made sense

indicators.note: possibly means the letters given could be arranged another way
sending back means the pudding word is read backwards

parts.note: pud is short for pudding, a dessert

explanation.surface: A dead person might send back the pudding course, which seemed sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges DEAD to ADDE, and 'sending back' turns PUD into DUP.
explanation.definitionFit: When figures or facts add up, they are consistent and logical, so 'added up' is an idiom for made sense.

clue.text: Sketch of partial rail strike?

definitions.meaning: a rough drawing of the main lines
a strike on only one railway route: the staff on that line are out

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word: one line out, a strike affecting only part of the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawing of just the contours of a shape is a sketch, the same word naming a summary of main points.

clue.text: 1 or 2, say, in between

indicators.note: in means the abbreviation goes inside the word for between

parts.note: inter is a Latin-derived prefix meaning between
eg (for example) is signalled by say

explanation.surface: A number like one or two, say, falls in between.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' is EG (for example), not part of the definition, which ends at '1 or 2'.
explanation.definitionFit: One and two are whole numbers, examples of the class of whole numbers mathematicians call integers.

clue.text: Eastern spider (not northern) causes problem with organ

indicators.note: not means the letter for northern is left out of the spider's name

parts.note: Arachne was the weaver in Greek myth turned into a spider by Athena

explanation.surface: An oriental spider, not from the north, causes trouble with a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' looks musical; it is the ear. 'causes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain in the ear, a body organ, is a medical complaint, a problem affecting that organ.

clue.text: Shakespearean tear, singular medicine for seer

definitions.meaning: Shakespeare uses this compound in Henry IV Part 2 for a single tear falling from the eye
one of the drops of liquid medicine put in the eye, a seer here being anyone who sees

explanation.walkthrough: 'seer' looks like a prophet but is just someone who sees; 'singular' asks for the one-drop form.
explanation.definitionFit: A single drop of eye medicine is named by the same compound Shakespeare used for one tear from the eye.

clue.text: Displace journalist that has complaint about energy

parts.note: ed is short for editor, a journalist

indicators.note: about means the ailment wraps around the energy symbol

parts.note: gout is a painful complaint of the joints
e is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: An editor with an ailment has lost his energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that has' joins the editor to the complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: To edge someone out is to push them aside gradually and take their place, which is to displace them.

clue.text: Painter and composer with a missing novelist from Italy

indicators.note: missing means the letter a is left out of the composer's name

parts.note: Edward Elgar was the English composer of the Enigma Variations
Umberto Eco was the Italian author of The Name of the Rose

explanation.surface: An artist and a composer, minus something, joined by an Italian writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' and 'with' only join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: El Greco was the Cretan-born painter of the Spanish Renaissance, so he is a painter.

clue.text: See 13
Bertram, the suitor, embracing holy one

indicators.note: embracing means the suitor wraps around the saint

parts.note: a wooer is a man courting someone, a suitor
st is short for saint, a holy person

explanation.surface: Bertram the lover hugs a saint.
explanation.walkthrough: Bertram Wooster is P G Wodehouse's comic hero, Bertie, valeted by Jeeves; 'the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie Wooster's full first name in P G Wodehouse's stories is Bertram, so the forename stands for him.

clue.text: Comedian removing pole from hood

indicators.note: removing means the letter for a pole is taken out of the criminal word

parts.note: a hood, short for hoodlum, is a gangster
n stands for north, one of the earth's poles

explanation.surface: A comic takes a stick out of a hood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hood' looks like headgear but is American slang for a gangster; 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A gagster tells gags, jokes, so he is a comedian or joke-teller.

clue.text: Measure used by the Marines

parts.note: RM stands for the Royal Marines

explanation.surface: A measure the Marines use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used by' is a link; a therm is a unit of heat once used on British gas bills.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a unit of heat energy, a measure equal to 100,000 British thermal units.

clue.text: Object to feeble note

parts.note: a thin excuse is a feeble one
G is a musical note

explanation.surface: Raise an objection to a weak musical note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a verb, to protest; it is the noun. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing is any physical object or item, so the two words are synonyms as nouns.

clue.text: Copies around the home counties initiate such proximity

indicators.note: around means the copies go about the abbreviation for the region

parts.note: clones are identical copies
SE, south-east England, is where the home counties around London lie

indicators.note: initiate means the opening letter, the one that starts the word, is taken

explanation.surface: Duplicates around London's commuter belt begin a sense of nearness.
explanation.walkthrough: The home counties are the counties surrounding London, in the south-east (SE) of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Closeness is nearness in space, the same as proximity.

clue.text: Burke's non-U crime: arrest will result

definitions.note: read as 'Burke is', so the definition stands for a noun phrase naming what Burke was

indicators.note: will result signals that a new arrangement of the letters comes out of the words before

explanation.surface: A crime unbecoming a gentleman leads to a police arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: William Burke and William Hare murdered people in 1820s Edinburgh to sell the bodies for dissection; 'non-U' is British slang for not upper-class.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave robbers who supplied corpses to anatomists were called this; Burke, a murderer for the same trade, is the famous case.
